sentences.text: Iguanodon was a large, bulky herbivore that could reach lengths of 9 to 11 meters and weigh up to 4.5 metric tons.
These bulky herbivores were capable of shifting between bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion.
The animal possessed a toothless, scoop-shaped lower jaw symphysis that resembles that of two-toed sloths and the extinct ground sloth Mylodon.
Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins held a banquet for twenty people inside the standing Iguanodon sculpture before it was completed.
Iguanodon could reach a maximum speed of 24 km/h when moving bipedally but could not gallop as a quadruped.
Iguanodon is one of the three genera originally used to define the group Dinosauria, alongside Megalosaurus and Hylaeosaurus.
The genus Iguanodon was named in 1825 by English geologist Gideon Mantell based on fossils found in England.
A popular legend claims Mary Ann Mantell discovered the first Iguanodon teeth in Tilgate Forest in 1822, though evidence suggests Gideon Mantell found them himself.
Gideon Mantell realized in 1849 that Iguanodon had slender forelimbs rather than being heavy, pachyderm-like animals.
Early reconstructions of Iguanodon incorrectly placed a horn on its nose, which was later identified as a modified thumb.
Early reconstructions depicted Iguanodon as a quadrupedal beast with a horn on its nose.
Originally thought to be on the nose, the thumb spike of Iguanodon was correctly identified as a modified thumb on the hand by Dollo.
With a straight tail and back, Iguanodon likely walked with its body held horizontally to the ground, using its arms to support itself if necessary.
David Norman suggested a diet of horsetails, cycads, and conifers.
However, iguanodontians in general have been related to the rise of angiosperm plants in the Cretaceous due to inferred dinosaur habits.
The size of the largest species, like I. bernissartensis, would have allowed it to access food from the ground up to 4 to 5 meters high in trees.
A fossil specimen of Iguanodon shows evidence of a fractured hip bone and an injury to the ischium.
Two other Iguanodon individuals exhibited osteoarthritis, indicated by bone overgrowths known as osteophytes in their anklebones.
Research published in 2026 interprets Iguanodon bernissartensis as likely an obligate quadruped.
New information regarding the variability of cranial morphology in Iguanodon was provided by a 2026 study.
Iguanodon belongs to the larger group Iguanodontia, which also includes duck-billed hadrosaurs.
Iguanodon gives its name to the clade Iguanodontia, a populous group of ornithopods known from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous.
The Maidstone specimen, known as the Mantel-piece and labeled NHMUK 3741, was excluded from the genus Iguanodon.
The exact function of Iguanodon thumb spikes is debated, with hypotheses suggesting they were used for defense or foraging.
In 2026, Rotatori and colleagues suggested that Delapparentia is a distinct taxon related to Magnamanus and I. galvensis, proposing a new genus name for the latter.
Iguanodon lived during the early Lower Cretaceous period, between 126 and 120 million years ago (Barremian to Aptian stages), in what is now Europe.
Iguanodon lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 154.8 and 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether Dollo's reconstruction of Iguanodon was accurate, as the tail was likely straight rather than bent, supported by evidence of ossified tendons.
Fossil evidence from Nehden showing a wide range of ages suggests Iguanodon bernissartensis may have lived in groups.
New analyses indicate at least three high-mortality events occurred over a geologically brief period of 10 to 100 years, though this does not necessarily prove herd living.
